text: Carlo Antonio Tavella came from Milan, the son of a Genoese merchant, and worked mainly in Genoa as a Baroque painter. He was first a pupil of Giuseppe Merati, then of a painter known as il Solfarolo. In 1695 he worked with the Dutch painter Pieter Mulier II, also known as il Tempesta. Later he painted landscapes for Alessandro Magnasco and for Domenico and Paolo Piola, and he helped decorate Palazzo Franchi in Genoa. His daughter Angiola was a painter too. He died in Genoa in 1738.

Étienne Terrus went to Paris to study at seventeen but soon went back to Elne, where he produced most of his works. He used to walk with his easel and is considered one of the precursors of Fauvism. Artists such as Georges-Daniel de Monfreid, André Derain and Henri Matisse admired him, and Matisse was his penpal from 1905 to 1917. In 1994 a museum about him was inaugurated in his birth town. He was a French painter from Roussillon.

Eva Watson-Schütze was one of the founding members of the Photo-Secession. She was born Eva Lawrence Watson in Jersey City, New Jersey, the youngest of four children, though little else is known about her family or early childhood. In 1883, at sixteen, she enrolled at the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts in Philadelphia and studied under Thomas Eakins. Her interests then were watercolor and oil painting. Around the 1890s she began to develop a passion for photography and decided to make it her career.

Faustino Anderloni was one of seven children of a wealthy farmer in Brescia, and he helped train his youngest brother Pietro, who also became an engraver. While studying in his hometown he developed an early interest in scientific and educational illustration. By 1782 he had produced a few plates for a work on anatomy by Antonio Scarpa, published in Pavia. In 1784 he moved to Pavia to oversee the illustrations for two more of Scarpa's works, on the nervous system and on bones. He also made plates for a major treatise on zoology and botany by Giovanni Antonio Scopoli.

George Roux is best known for the illustrations he made for Jules Verne's science-fiction novels in the series Les voyages extraordinaires. He was the second-most prolific illustrator of Verne's novels, after Léon Benett, and he drew the pictures for 22 novels in the original editions published by Pierre-Jules Hetzel. The first of them was L'Épave du Cynthia in 1885. The last was L'Étonnante aventure de la mission Barsac in 1919. He also illustrated André Laurie's Axel Ebersen for the Boy's Own Paper.

Daniël Haringh lived and died in Loosduinen, a painter from the Dutch Republic. According to the RKD, he was a pupil of Arnold van Ravesteyn and Caspar Netscher from 1664 to 1669, and in 1669 he became a member of the Confrerie Pictura. He is known for portraits and interior decorations. His pupils were Richard van Bleeck, Michiel Godijn, Abraham van Hoogstraten and Dirk Kindt.

Gertrude Käsebier became known for her images of motherhood, her portraits of Native Americans and her promotion of photography as a career for women. Born Gertrude Stanton in Fort Des Moines, now Des Moines, Iowa, she was the daughter of John W. Stanton, who moved a sawmill to Golden, Colorado, at the start of the Pike's Peak Gold Rush. He prospered from the building boom that followed. In 1860, at eight, she travelled with her mother and younger brother to join him. That year he was elected the first mayor of Golden, then the capital of the Colorado Territory.

Giuseppe Bonati, also known as Giovannino del Pio, trained first under Francesco Costanzo Cattaneo and Leonello Bononi. His patron, Cardinal Carlo Pio di Savoia, sent him to Bologna in 1658 to train with Guercino. In 1662 he went to Rome to work in the studio of Pier Francesco Mola, and he tried to establish a studio to rival Carlo Maratta. He travelled through Italy with his patrons, including a stay in Venice, and returned to Rome in 1665. There he worked in many churches, among them Santa Croce in Gerusalemme and Santa Maria in Vallicella.

Heinrich Maria von Hess belonged to the Nazarene movement. His father, the engraver Carl Ernst Christoph Hess, brought him up to art and accompanied the Düsseldorf academy when the Bavarian elector, raised to a kingship by Napoleon, moved it to Munich. Heinrich studied at the Academy in Munich from 1813 to 1817 under Johann Peter von Langer. His skills and reputation attracted the attention of King Maximilian, who sent him to Rome in 1821 with a stipend. During his four years there he came under the influence of Johann Friedrich Overbeck.

Johann Lukas von Hildebrandt studied in Rome under Carlo Fontana. He then built fortresses for Prince Eugene of Savoy during his Italian campaigns and became his favourite architect. In 1700 he became court engineer in Vienna, in 1711 head of the court department of building, and in 1723 court architect. His designs for palaces, gardens, churches and villas were widely imitated, and his architectural principles spread across central and southeast Europe. Among his works are the Palais Schwarzenberg and the Belvedere.

Antonio Zucchi married the painter Angelica Kauffman in 1781, and late in life she moved with him to Rome. Born in Venice, he studied under his uncle Carlo Zucchi and later with Francesco Fontebasso and Jacopo Amigoni. In Rome he made etchings of capricci and views of classical buildings and ruins. He worked with Robert Adam on decorating houses in England, among them Kenwood and Osterley Park. In 1770 he was elected an associate of the Royal Academy. Lady Boringdon commissioned ceilings from him.

Louise Hersent-Mauduit painted portraits and historical scenes in oil. Her works were shown at the Paris Salon from 1810, and she received first-class medals at the Salons of 1817 and 1819. Jean Baptiste Tardieu engraved several of them. She was born in Paris, the daughter of the architect and mathematician Antoine-René Mauduit. She studied under Charles Meynier and possibly her husband, the painter Louis Hersent, who was also notable for portraits and history paintings.

Paolo da San Leocadio, an Italian painter from Reggio Emilia, was mostly active in Spain. He moved to Ferrara, where local painters such as Bono da Ferrara and Ercole de' Roberti influenced him. In 1472 he sailed from Ostia to Valencia for Cardinal Rodrigo Borgia, the future Pope Alexander VI. In 1506 he painted, with Francesco Pagano, the doors of the high altar of the cathedral of Valencia, with subjects from the Life of the Virgin. His Virgin of the Knight of Montesa is in the Prado, and his Holy Conversation is in the National Gallery in London.

Salomon Rombouts was the son of the landscape painter Gillis Rombouts and, like his father, painted landscapes and beach scenes. Two earlier brothers, also named Salomon, died in infancy, which has led to some confusion about his date of birth being 1652. He travelled to Italy in 1681 and is registered in Florence for several years. He died, perhaps in Italy, before 1702, when Vincent van der Vinne's son recorded him as deceased in a list of members of the Haarlem Guild of St. Luke.

Samuel Worcester Rowse was most famous for his drawings of Ralph Waldo Emerson and Henry David Thoreau. He is also well known for his lithograph The Resurrection of Henry Box Brown at Philadelphia. Born in Bath, Maine, he worked there as an engraver. In 1852 he worked for a lithographer and then opened a studio in Boston, because his crayon and charcoal portraits were in demand. He boarded with the family of Emerson in the summer of 1854 and sketched Thoreau, whom Sophia Thoreau thought well captured.

Max Wilhelm Roman made a study trip to Italy in 1871 with his teacher and painted some of his first landscapes in Olevano Romano. It was the first of many such trips throughout his life. His father was a senior civil servant, and he completed his initial studies in Nuremberg. He later settled in Karlsruhe, where he studied for nine years at the Academy of Fine Arts under Hans Fredrik Gude and Eugen Bracht. With his older brother Victor, a drawing teacher, he often made excursions through the Black Forest, sketching farms and villages.

Mina Carlson-Bredberg is particularly well known for her portraits and scenes from contemporary life. She was born in Stockholm to wealthy parents, and her uncle was the newspaper publisher and critic Lars Johan Hierta. As a teenager she took private painting lessons from Kerstin Cardon and Elisabeth Keyser. At twenty, social convention obliged her to marry a family friend, Vilhelm Swalin, after she was seen kissing him, and for the seven years of the marriage she gave up painting. She left in 1885 for Paris. There she resumed her training.

Niccolò Codazzi painted architectural pictures, capricci and vedute, and he also made decorative frescoes as a painter of quadratura. He was the son of the architectural painter Viviano Codazzi and trained with him, later working in his father's workshop. The early works of father and son are difficult to tell apart. His family relocated to Rome after the anti-Spanish revolt of Masaniello in 1647. Niccolò was in Rome from 1675. He was active in Paris and Genoa too.

Charles Laplante became one of the main interpreters of Gustave Doré as a wood engraver and illustrator. He was born in Sèvres, studied with Jules Fagnion and exhibited from 1861. He engraved Adrienne Faguet's drawings for Louis Figuier's Histoire des plantes. He worked for the Hetzel editions, notably on Jules Verne's novels, alongside Henri Théophile Hildibrand and Charles Barbant. He also interpreted drawings by Philippoteaux for books by Alphonse Daudet and by Erckmann-Chatrian, as well as drawings by Émile Bayard.

Charles-Louis Houdard produced many etchings and aquatints and was an adept of Japonisme. He studied at the École des beaux-arts in Paris in the ateliers of Edmond Yon, Gustave Boulanger and Jules Lefebvre. He began producing in 1886 and showed a painting called Sur la plage, à Menton at the Salon des indépendants in 1888. One of his first prints was published in L'Estampe originale. The gallery of Siegfried Bing in Paris represented him at the Salon de l'Art nouveau. He became known mainly for colour prints that combine etching and aquatint.

Theodor Hoffbauer made many views and dioramas showing how the famous buildings of Paris once looked, and the public could see them in exhibitions. He designed the reconstructions himself and had several draughtsmen and engravers help execute them. His credible views of the Louvre, the Châtelet, the Maison du Temple, the Bastille prison and the abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés were published in Paris à travers les âges, alongside texts by historians of Paris. Born in Düsseldorf, he was a French painter of German origin, and also an architect.

Francisco Lacoma y Fontanet studied at the Lonja drawing school in Barcelona, where he excelled at flower painting under Salvador Molet. In 1804 the Junta pensioned him to continue his studies in Paris, where the Peninsular War broke out. Politics did not stop him from showing works at the Paris salons and meeting Spaendonck, David and Gros, who influenced his style. After the war he took part in diplomatic efforts to get back the artworks French troops had taken from Spain, which in 1819 earned him a place in the Royal Academy of San Fernando.

Fredrik Borgen was the son of a farmer. From 1870 he attended the painting school of Johan Fredrik Eckersberg in Kristiania, and Morten Müller, who ran the school after Eckersberg's death, taught him from 1871. Peder Cappelen Thurmann was also his teacher. At first he greatly admired the painting of Hans Fredrik Gude and Amaldus Nielsen, and later Charlotte von Krogh, Edvard Diriks and Gerhard Munthe influenced him. He exhibited his landscapes from 1873.

George Vincent is considered one of the most talented painters of the Norwich School. He was born in Norwich in 1796 and died around 1832. As a landscape painter he produced watercolours, etchings and oil paintings, based on Dutch landscape painting and on the style of John Crome. The son of a weaver, he studied at Norwich Grammar School and was then apprenticed to Crome. The school's reputation outside East Anglia in the 1820s rests largely on the work of George and his friend James Stark.

Jacopo Confortini, son of the painter Matteo and younger brother of Pietro, trained in the family and then with established Florentine artists such as Giovanni Bilivert and Matteo Rosselli. He obtained Florentine citizenship in 1617. At barely twenty he took part in decorating the Medici casino of San Marco, where he met the eccentric Giovanni da San Giovanni. He enrolled in the Arte del Disegno in 1629 and received numerous religious and secular commissions. In the payments for the frescoes in the refectory of Santa Trinita, where he worked beside Giovanni da San Giovanni, he is recorded as Frate Confortini.

Jan van Cleve was born in Venlo in 1646, according to Flament the son of Gabriel van Cleef, a soldier in Spanish service. He left Venlo for Brussels to learn painting, working first for Louis Cousin and then for Gaspar de Crayer, whose style his own resembles. He certainly worked on paintings by De Crayer and copied them. He painted historical genre pieces and religious scenes, and he gained fame in the Southern Netherlands at the end of the 17th century and the start of the 18th. He died in Ghent in 1716.

Joaquín Turina y Areal trained at the School of Fine Arts in Seville, born there in 1847, and from 1879 took part in exhibitions in Seville and Cádiz. He won a gold medal at the Cádiz exhibition that year. His work focuses on scenes of everyday life, historical themes and religious painting, in an amiable, colourful style with some romantic touches within its realism. He was the father of the musician Joaquín Turina Pérez. He died in Seville in 1903.

Kasper Järnefelt was the eldest of nine children, and his siblings included the painter Eero, the composer Armas and Aino, who married Sibelius. Born in Saint Petersburg in 1859, he worked as a film critic, a promoter of literature, a government translator and teacher of Russian, and a painter. He was important as a translator, given the developments between Finland and Russia in the last decades of the 19th century. He worked with the writer Juhani Aho. He studied art at the Finnish Art Academy and at the university.

Lambertus Lingeman was born in Amsterdam and became a pupil of Petrus Franciscus Greive. In 1853 he became a member of Arti et Amicitiae, serving as its treasurer for nine years and later as chairman for a year. He lived and worked in Amsterdam, Baarn, Hilversum and finally Abcoude-Baambrugge. He painted mainly genre scenes, mostly scenes from the 17th century. He took part in exhibitions in Amsterdam and The Hague and in the world's fair in Philadelphia in 1876.

Mariano Pedrero began his career as a drawing teacher at the San José lyceum in Torrelavega and later became its director. He published in the press of Cantabria before moving to Madrid in 1898. There he became art director of the magazine Nuevo Mundo and made his first two covers, on the war in Cuba. In 1903 he was named art editor of La Ilustración Española y Americana. He was a Spanish draughtsman, painter, poster artist and illustrator, born in Burgos and raised in the province of Santander.

Parrasio Micheli descended from an aristocratic Venetian family and may have begun his training in Titian's workshop, as indirect sources suggest. One is a letter from Micheli to King Philip II, in which he declared that Titian was the reference for all his studies. His few documented surviving works, all from an advanced stage of his career, show firm adherence to the models of Paolo Veronese. According to Freedberg, he was one of Veronese's most obvious imitators, but also the least skilful. In 1563 he received an important commission for a large canvas dedicated to a doge.

Philippe Cardon, a Belgian draughtsman, was the second child of the painter and engraver Antoine Cardon the Elder. His brother Anthony became an engraver with a fine career in England, and his uncle Jean-Guillain Cardon was a musician, composer and violinist who made his name at the court of Versailles. Baptized in Brussels, Philippe was described as a painter at the time he married Catherine Antoinette De Schmid there. They had two known children.

Sebastián López de Arteaga introduced the naturalistic style to New Spain. Born in Seville, he was the son of a painter of the same name who died the year he was born, and his mother, Inés de los Reyes, saw to his training. Nothing is known of his apprenticeship, but he passed the master's examination in the Seville painters' guild in 1630. He ran his own workshop there until 1638, with up to three apprentices. In 1640 he sailed with the fleet of the viceroy Diego López Pacheco to New Spain, now Mexico.
